entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
Simon & Schuster, founded in 1924 in New York City by Richard Simon and M. Lincoln Schuster, became one of America's major publishing houses famous for publishing crossword puzzle books (their founding product), Ernest Hemingway, P.G. Wodehouse, and Joseph Heller's Catch-22. The company pioneered mass market paperbacks and audio books in America, and its subsequent corporate ownership (Gulf+Western, Paramount, Viacom, CBS, then Kohlberg Kravis Roberts) represents the Hollywood-media industry's consolidation of publishing.

Simon & Schuster was founded after Richard Simon's aunt asked him to find crossword puzzle books — discovering none existed, Simon and Schuster published The Cross Word Puzzle Book (1924), which became a bestseller and launched the American crossword puzzle craze. This accidental founding revealed both publishers' entrepreneurial instincts for popular culture that distinguished their house from more literary competitors.

S&S published Joseph Heller's Catch-22 (1961), one of the most significant American novels of the 20th century, after multiple rejections elsewhere. The publisher's list has included F. Scott Fitzgerald (The Last Tycoon), Ernest Hemingway (A Farewell to Arms), and prominent political works. The 2023 attempt by Penguin Random House to acquire Simon & Schuster for $2.175 billion was blocked by the US Department of Justice as anticompetitive — the first major publisher merger blocked by antitrust enforcement — leading to KKR's $1.62 billion acquisition instead.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Simon & Schuster's publication of Catch-22 and the DOJ's blocking of its Penguin Random House acquisition — the first major publisher merger blocked on antitrust grounds — make it central to two defining moments in American publishing history.
